summary: Defines jCard, a JSON format for vCard data, which represents information about people and entities such as phone numbers, emails, names and addresses. This makes vCard data easier to use in JSON-based applications.

eli5.summary: An address book entry written in a format programs on the web like.

questions: how to convert vcard to json
what is the vcard json media type
subtitle: How to write an address-book card (vCard) as plain JSON so web code can read it easily.

tldr.problem: vCard is a text format for contact data, but it is awkward for JavaScript widgets and web applications to process.
tldr.mechanism: jCard maps every vCard property, parameter and value onto JSON arrays, objects and strings with fixed rules, so converting to jCard and back keeps the same meaning.
tldr.outcome: Contact data can be handled by ordinary JSON parsers and travels as the application/vcard+json media type. RFC 7095 is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted.

today: RFC 7095 is a Proposed Standard from January 2014. Its metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC, so it remains the definition of jCard.

sections.title: Why a JSON Form of vCard
sections.content:
The vCard format (RFC 6350) captures and exchanges the kind of information kept in an address book or directory. jCard is a JSON format for the same data. The RFC says the main advantage is easier processing for JavaScript-based widgets and libraries, especially in web applications.

It is a sibling of jCal, a JSON format for iCalendar (RFC 5545), and shares its design goals with jCal and xCal (RFC 6321). Round-tripping a vCard to jCard and back must give the same semantic result, and all components, properties and parameters are preserved. Element order and the case of names are not necessarily preserved. Extensions to vCard must not require an update to jCard.
sections.eli5: jCard writes an address-book card in a format that web programs read easily. If you turn it back into the old format, nothing important is lost.

sections.title: The jCard Object and Properties
sections.content:
A vCard is made of properties, each with a value and zero or more parameters. In jCard the whole card is an array of two elements: the string "vcard" and an array of properties. The vCard BEGIN and END lines MUST NOT appear as properties; they are added back when converting to vCard.

Each property is an array with three fixed elements followed by the value or values: the property name in lowercase, an object holding the parameters (empty if none), and the lowercase type identifier of the value. A single-valued property therefore has exactly four elements. A multi-valued property such as categories simply carries more value elements.

The version property MUST be present, with the same value as in the vCard (4.0 for RFC 6350), and MUST be the first property.
sections.eli5: Each fact on the card is a little list: its name, any extra notes, what kind of thing it is, and then the actual value.

sections.title: Structured Values, Groups and Parameters
sections.content:
Some vCard properties, such as ADR and N, hold structured values split by semicolons. In jCard these become an array with one element per component, and empty components are zero-length strings. If a component itself has several values, it is a nested array. The array MUST keep all required elements, even empty ones. A structured value with just one component SHOULD be written as a single text value, so parsers SHOULD check whether a value is an array or a primitive.

Parameters become a JSON object whose keys are lowercase parameter names; the case of values is kept. Parameters that take a comma-separated list in vCard MUST be arrays of strings in jCard, for example sort-as. The VALUE parameter MUST NOT appear in the object, because the type identifier already says the type.

vCard property groups (a prefix and a dot, such as CONTACT.FN) are replaced by a group parameter, and property names in jCard MUST NOT carry a group prefix.
sections.eli5: An address with street, town and country becomes a list with a slot for each part. If a part is missing, its slot is left empty so everything stays in the right place.

sections.title: Value Types and Conversion Order
sections.content:
When converting vCard to jCard, lines MUST first be unfolded, then vCard escaping MUST be removed, then JSON escaping MUST be applied. Going back reverses the order, and long lines SHOULD be folded.

Each vCard value type has a jCard type identifier: text, uri, date, time, date-time, date-and-or-time, timestamp, boolean, integer, float, utc-offset and language-tag. Booleans and numbers use JSON booleans and numbers, and the rest are JSON strings.

Dates and times use the extended format of ISO 8601, which adds separators. For example, the vCard date 19850412 becomes 1985-04-12, and the time 232050 becomes 23:20:50. A UTC offset gets a colon between hours and minutes. Unlike jCal, jCard permits UTC offsets inside time values. Decimals and exponents in an integer, and exponents in a float, MUST be removed when converting back to vCard.
sections.eli5: Dates and times get neat dashes and colons, like writing 1985-04-12 instead of a run of digits, and numbers become real numbers.

sections.title: Unknown Properties and the unknown Type
sections.content:
A converter may meet a new property or an X- extension property whose default value type it does not know. To keep it safe, such a property, when it has no VALUE parameter, MUST become a plain JSON string holding the unprocessed value text, and its type MUST be set to unknown. Using text instead could add escaping that breaks round-tripping.

Going the other way, a value of type unknown MUST NOT get a VALUE parameter, and its value MUST be taken over into vCard without processing. An unrecognized parameter is converted to a string, as if it were text. Extension names are lowercased, so X-FOO becomes x-foo.

The UNKNOWN value type is reserved for jCard and MUST NOT be used in any vCard.
sections.eli5: If the converter sees something it does not understand, it copies it over exactly as written and labels it unknown, so it can be put back later unchanged.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the mapping is one-to-one, so it does not change the meaning of the data or add or remove security considerations of the underlying vCard data, including those in Section 9 of RFC 6350. JSON brings its own risks, covered in RFC 4627: a flaw in a JSON parser could be a threat that plain vCard does not have.

Implementations should use a native parser with full awareness of JSON. Using JavaScript eval() is allowed only with the regular expression check from RFC 4627. The RFC also expects vCard data to be disseminated more widely, for example in web applications rather than dedicated contact managers.
sections.eli5: Reading the card with a careful, proper reader is safer than running the text like a program.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media type application/vcard+json. It takes an optional version parameter as defined for text/vcard, and follows the encoding rules of application/json. It is intended for common use, with no restrictions.

It also adds two reservations to the vCard registries: the GROUP parameter and the UNKNOWN value data type. Both are reserved for jCard and MUST NOT be used in plain vCard. A group value must use only letters, digits and hyphens, and MUST NOT be empty.
sections.eli5: The format gets its own official label, and two special words are set aside so that old-style cards never use them.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content: Appendix B converts the vCard of Simon Perreault, the author of RFC 6350, into jCard. The name becomes ["n", {}, "text", ["Perreault", "Simon", "", "", ["ing. jr", "M.Sc."]]], with empty strings for empty components and a nested array for the two suffixes. A phone line with TYPE="work,voice" becomes a type parameter holding ["work", "voice"], and the TZ value -0500 becomes the utc-offset value -05:00.
sections.eli5: The example shows one real contact card side by side in both styles, so you can see each piece land in its new place.
